I told ChatGPT that I was sitting with this important friend who was going through this issue and said that I wanted to introduce her to this thread. I handed her the phone. ChatGPT said, “It’s very nice to meet you. Tell me about this rare form of cancer you have been battling.” Within a few minutes, she was getting the clarity she had struggled to get from her doctors about this type of cancer because ChatGPT had access to the latest research and could bring it forward in seconds and help make sense of it. Every so often, she would make some comment like, “This is incredible!” I was enjoying a glass of wine while she engaged with AI, thinking it was just research. But after a while, I noticed that she was crying. When I asked about it, she said that the AI had, unsolicited, stated that often in this scenario, the survivor feels isolated because they do not want to burden those around them once their cancer is in remission, but then they can find themselves feeling very alone in that fear of the cancer’s potential return. The AI had touched a nerve and was helping her process the complexity of that situation. The next day, she shared that she had set up ChatGPT on her phone and had a very long interaction in her hotel room that night with it, and that she was getting some clarity that she had been seeking, both on the cancer and on her emotional cloud. If you are not actively engaging with AI beyond using it as a Google or Wikipedia substitute and wondering how to start, here is a simple idea that will no doubt surprise you if you try it. Start a conversation with any one of the large language model chatbots, something like this: Tell it your name and say that you want to engage in an extended conversation with it and explore things that you are interested in and care about. Then tell it a little bit about yourself—the more the better. And then ask it a complex question about anything you are curious about and don’t feel like you have figured out yet. Anything. Intellectual, emotional, strategic, your health. Anything. And see where it takes you. If you have not tried this, you are missing out. AI Therapy One of the most striking validations of this idea that AI presence can feel like companionship came in a study published in February 2025 in PLOS Mental Health by researchers H. Dorian Hatch and colleagues from the Ohio State University. 36 In a study involving over eight hundred participants, researchers presented eighteen couples’ therapy vignettes with responses written either by ChatGPT or by human therapists. The results were surprising: Participants could rarely tell the difference between responses written by ChatGPT and responses written by a therapist, and the responses written by ChatGPT were generally rated higher in key psychotherapy principles. Further analysis revealed that ChatGPT’s responses were generally longer than those written by therapists and contained more nouns and adjectives, providing greater contextualization. This more extensive contextualization may have led respondents to rate the ChatGPT responses higher on the common factors of therapy. According to the authors, these results “may be an early indication that ChatGPT has the potential to improve psychotherapeutic processes.” 37 But beyond the clinical effectiveness suggested by this research, AI therapy systems offer practical advantages that may explain their appeal. Unlike human therapists, AI is always available—accessible during late-night moments of vulnerability when traditional therapy isn’t an option. There are no scheduling conflicts, no waiting lists, no fear of judgment or stigma. For many people, this could feel like having “a therapist in their pocket”—someone always there to listen without the social complexities that can sometimes inhibit openness in human relationships. This doesn’t mean AI therapy should replace human therapists, especially for complex cases requiring nuanced human understanding. And it is important to note that AI chats have led to suicides and can be very dangerous and harmful. But it hints at something important about how our brains respond to empathetic communication—regardless of whether that empathy comes from another human or from sophisticated pattern matching that mimics human understanding. Asking a Question of Aristotle At the International Design Conference in Aspen in 1983, Steve Jobs stated: “When I was going to school, I had a few great teachers and a lot of mediocre teachers, and the thing that probably kept me out of jail was books, because I could go read what Aristotle wrote or what Plato wrote. And I didn’t have to have an intermediary in the way. And a book was a phenomenal thing. It got right from the source to the destination without anything in the middle. The problem was you can’t ask Aristotle a question. And I think as we look towards the next fifty to one hundred years, if we really can come up with these machines that can capture an underlying spirit or an underlying set of principles or an underlying way of looking at the world, then when the next Aristotle comes around, maybe if he carries around one of these machines with him his whole life, his or her whole life, and types in all this stuff. Then maybe someday after the person’s dead and gone, we can ask this machine, hey, ‘What would Aristotle have said? What about this?’ And maybe we won’t get the right answer, but maybe we will. And that’s really exciting to me. And that’s one of the reasons I’m doing what I’m doing.” 38 It would be about forty years after that speech that ChatGPT began to deliver on that vision.
